# Rājovādajātaka (Ja 334)

**ID:** Ja 334
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Rājovādajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Rājovādajātaka* (Ja 334) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Catukkanipāta* (Fours) of the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883]. The framing narrative is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivered the teaching concerning the admonition of a king, noting that the full introductory story is given in the *Tesakuṇajātaka* [Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the King of Benares travels incognito throughout his realm seeking to discover his own faults, but finds only praise [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. Venturing into the Himalayas, he encounters the Bodhisatta living as a forest ascetic, who presents him with sweet wild banyan figs (*nigrodhapakka*) [UNDV 2009; Fausböll 1883]. The Bodhisatta explains that when a ruler governs justly and righteously (*dhammena*), nature flourishes and products such as honey, molasses, and wild fruits maintain their natural sweetness and potency, whereas an unjust ruler causes nature to turn bitter and infertile [UNDV 2009; IBC 2011; Emmanuel 2013].

The central didactic verse of the Jātaka employs the simile of a herd of cattle crossing a stream (*gavañ ce taramānānaṁ*): if the leading bull strays, the entire herd goes astray, but if the leader crosses straight, the rest follow safely; similarly, people follow the moral conduct of their king [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha identifies the king as Ānanda and the ascetic as himself [Fausböll 1883].

The verses of Ja 334 are directly parallel to the *Adhammikasutta* of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 4.70), sharing an extensive textual sequence (§1.1–4.6) [DharmaNexus]. They also appear verbatim in two later Jātakas, the *Ummādantījātaka* (Ja 527) and the *Mahābodhijātaka* (Ja 528), and are cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (*Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, Ne 37) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus further detects verse alignments with the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada*, the *Kavidappaṇanīti*, and chapters on righteous kingship in Tibetan translations of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
